messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark is a fifty-three-year-old social worker who has worked for two decades in community outreach, visiting clients in housing projects and shelters. Eight months ago, during an evening home visit in an unfamiliar high-rise, he was cornered in the building’s dimly lit stairwell and sexually assaulted by a man he had never seen before. The attack was sudden, silent, and over in minutes, but the terror did not fade. In the weeks afterward, Mark found himself unable to speak about what had happened—he knew the facts but could not find words to shape them into a story he could tell his wife or his supervisor. Opening his mouth to describe the assault made his throat close, and a wave of shame that felt physical would wash over him, as though he himself had done something wrong.

When the memory surfaced without warning—the cold concrete wall against his back, the pressure of a hand over his mouth—Mark felt the same raw terror he had experienced in that stairwell. To cope, he began pushing the images out of his mind the instant they appeared, mentally slamming a door on them. Yet the harder he pushed, the more the memories seemed to linger at the edges of his thoughts, and he found himself ruminating in a different direction: how to get even with the assailant, imagining scenarios of tracking him down, confronting him, making him pay. This revenge rumination gave Mark a fleeting sense of control, but it also kept the assault alive in his mind, reinforcing the belief that danger was still near.

That sense of threat soon coloured everything. Walking to his car after work, Mark started checking behind him every few steps, certain that someone was following him. He stopped accepting new cases that required visiting unfamiliar neighbourhoods, because he could not assess the danger in a place he had never been before. Even routine delays began to feel ominous: when a meeting ran late or traffic slowed him down, his chest tightened and he assumed something bad was happening—another attack, another ambush. The hypervigilance, in turn, triggered more vivid intrusions. Each time he peered over his shoulder, the memory of the stairwell pressed closer, the shame and terror sharper. It became a cycle: the memory made him feel unsafe, so he scanned for threats, and the scanning brought the memory roaring back.

Mark’s avoidance of enclosed spaces grew more pronounced. He had always used the elevator at his office, but now he took the stairs—only to find that stairwells themselves were unbearable. He began arriving at work twenty minutes early to ensure he could take the main entrance and never be alone in a corridor. Thought suppression became a constant effort, but it left him exhausted and irritable, and his wife noticed he was withdrawing. He could not explain why he snapped when she asked about his day; the shame was too deep, the words too hard to reach. The revenge fantasies continued, but they offered no real relief—they only made the world feel more treacherous, as though the assailant were still out there, waiting for him to let his guard down. Mark’s professional life suffered when he refused to travel to a client’s unfamiliar apartment complex, citing vague discomfort. His supervisor expressed concern, and Mark knew he could not keep this up.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at home when his wife, holding his hand, asked him plainly why he kept looking over his shoulder even inside their own living room. Mark realised he had no safe place left. He is terrified that talking about the assault will break him open, but he is even more afraid of spending the rest of his life trapped in a shrinking world, always watching for an attacker who may never come—but whose shadow already fills every corridor he walks.
